query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superior wear resistance of high-entropy alloy protective coatings is controlled by the formation at elevated temperatures of a coherent, self‐adherent oxide layer (e.g., enriched in Al, Cr, or Ti) that serves as a low‐shear, hard barrier against mechanical abrasion.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) having a microstructure predisposed to rapid oxidation when exposed to oxygen at high temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose identical HEA coating samples to elevated temperature wear testing under two different atmospheres: an oxidizing (air) environment versus an inert (argon) atmosphere, or alternatively pre-oxidize some samples before wear testing.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating sliding wear tests performed at elevated temperatures (approximately 400–600 °C) where the kinetics allow for rapid oxide formation; the test environment is strictly controlled for oxygen content.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, coherent surface oxide layer (e.g., a mixture of protective oxides such as Cr2O3, Al2O3, or TiO2) that develops preferentially along phase boundaries or on elemental sites.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperature in an oxygen-rich environment, selected elements in the alloy oxidize to form a hard, low-shear protective film. This oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and lowers the friction coefficient, thereby attenuating wear. In the absence of oxygen (or with reduced oxide formation) the bare HEA surface is more prone to mechanical damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings tested in an oxidizing atmosphere will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced coefficients of friction compared to those tested under inert conditions, consistent with the presence of a coherent protective oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Under inert atmospheric conditions (or without pre-oxidation), minimal oxide formation occurs, leading to higher wear rates and friction levels as direct substrate contact dominates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA coatings whose composition includes elements capable of forming protective oxides, within a temperature range where oxidation kinetics are sufficiently activated (roughly 400–600 °C) and under wear conditions typical for protective coatings on high-temperature components.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature and composition of the protective oxide layer may vary with HEA composition, temperature, sliding speed, and environmental oxygen concentration. Quantitative effect sizes are uncertain without further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA coating samples. Subject one set to wear tests at elevated temperature (400–600 °C) in air to allow for oxide formation, and the other in a carefully controlled inert atmosphere (argon) to suppress oxidation. Characterize both sets pre- and post-test using microscopy and spectroscopy to detect the presence, continuity, and composition of surface oxide layers. Record wear rates and friction coefficients under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS or XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rates and friction coefficients in the oxidizing environment do not significantly improve compared to the inert atmosphere condition – or if no coherent, protective oxide layer is detected in the air-tested samples despite the operating temperature – then the hypothesized mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
